entries.proposition: Human reference rate: ethosuximide was recorded as effective in reducing absence frequency in about two thirds of those who received it (72 of 106), against valproate 102 of 142. The authors state the drugs were often prescribed for the whole epilepsy syndrome, so the percentages may reflect overall seizure burden and not absence-specific efficacy.
entries.snippet: The following treatments were reported as effective in reducing absence frequency: valproate (effective in 102/142, 72%), ethosuximide (in 72/106, 68%)

entries.proposition: Authors' own limit on the response percentages.
entries.snippet: We note that these medications were often prescribed to address the full epilepsy syndrome rather than absence seizures in isolation.

entries.proposition: The ethosuximide response differs by gene in small groups: for example SLC2A1 17 treated, 88 percent effective; SCN1A 9 treated, 78 percent; SYNGAP1 9 treated, 55 percent; CHD2 5 treated, 60 percent; CACNA1A 4 treated, 25 percent; NEXMIF 4 treated, 0 percent; SCN8A 2 treated, 100 percent. Counts are per-gene treated denominators; the table does not test heterogeneity across genes and several cells are 1 to 4 patients.
entries.anchor: Table 2 (Genetic etiology and treatment efficacy), NEXMIF row; the SLC2A1 row reads 17 (88%), the SCN1A row 9 (78%), the CACNA1A row 4 (25%) in the ETS column

entries.proposition: The SLC2A1 row of Table 2 gives ethosuximide in 17 treated with 88 percent effective, the highest among the genes with at least 10 patients.

A paediatric-onset human series is not a mechanistic test: the authors conclude traditional drugs including ethosuximide were commonly used and often effective, and that more than half the cohort remained drug-resistant. They draw no conclusion about the T-type mechanism or about why ethosuximide response differs by gene.
entries.snippet: Although traditional ASMs such as valproate and ethosuximide were commonly used and often effective in controlling absence seizures, more than half of the cohort remained drug‐resistant at last follow‐up

entries.proposition: Selection bias, in the authors' words: genetic testing was typically pursued in more severe phenotypes, so the high proportion with developmental disorder and drug resistance should not be generalised.
entries.snippet: We acknowledge that, considering the population of patients with absence seizures at large, our cohort is likely biased toward individuals with more severe phenotypes

entries.proposition: The cohort contains patients with developmental delay (54 percent), intellectual disability (65 percent) and drug-resistant epilepsy (54 percent). Predictors of poor developmental outcome were early developmental delay, drug resistance and early absence onset in a multivariable model; the series does not report whether ethosuximide response predicts or changes neurodevelopmental outcome.
entries.snippet: we confirmed early developmental delay, drug‐resistant epilepsy, and early absence onset as independent predictors of unfavorable outcomes (Table 3).
